entry.title: When Rule Downloads Lose Hostname Verification: CVE-2026-61812 in ModSecurity
entry.summary:
When Rule Downloads Lose Hostname Verification: CVE-2026-61812 in ModSecurity
Three of the four ModSecurity flaws patched in this batch affect how requests are inspected. CVE-2026-61812 affects how the engine gets its rules, and that is a different kind of risk. At disclosure the vendor had not yet published a severity score for it. CVE-2026-61812 was disclosed together with CVE-2026-73856, CVE-2026-73857 and CVE-2026-61813. The description states that a misconfigured libcurl setting weakens TLS hostname verification during remote rule downloads — listed in the advisory table as awaiting analysis. Remote rule sets let a ModSecurity deployment pull detection logic from a server rather than shipping it in a config file. That fetch uses libcurl, and it is supposed to validate both the certificate chain and the hostname in the certificate. The payoff for an attacker is control of the rule set. A malicious rule source can disable specific signatures, inject allow rules that exempt an attacker's traffic, or simply deliver a rule set that looks complete and is not. Because the engine treats downloaded rules as authoritative, the WAF keeps reporting that it is protecting the application. libmodsecurity3, versions 3.0.16 and earlier mod_security2, versions 2.9.14 and earlier Reachability depends entirely on whether the deployment downloads rules remotely. A deployment with a static, locally managed rule file is not affected by this flaw even on a vulnerable version. ZoomEye counts recorded for this topic: ModSecurity title matches 340, application-fingerprint matches 27, banner matches 1,700, body-text matches 777,209. A CVE-scoped query returns zero. Upgrade to libmodsecurity3 3.0.17 or mod_security2 2.9.15. ModSecurity Vulnerabilities: 4 WAF Bypasses Patched — https://securityonline.info/modsecurity-security-vulnerabilities/
OWASP ModSecurity project releases — https://github.com/owasp-modsecurity/ModSecurity/releases

entry.title: Nested Loops in a Python List Comprehension
entry.summary:
You can put more than one for in a list comprehension to get the effect of nested loops — but the order of those for clauses trips almost everyone up the first time. Here's how it actually works, with the one rule that makes it click. A comprehension with two for clauses behaves exactly like two nested for loops, and — this is the whole trick — the clauses read left to right in the same order you'd write the loops: outer loop first, inner loop second. pairs = [(x, y) for x in range(3) for y in range(3)] # [(0,0), (0,1), (0,2), (1,0), (1,1), (1,2), (2,0), (2,1), (2,2)]

entry.title: Collaborative Whiteboard Sync: Lease-Based Channel Lifecycles for Reliable State
entry.summary: Use a short-lived, server-authorized lease for every realtime channel, and make reconnect plus replay part of the protocol. That is the dependable choice for a collaborative whiteboard because a browser tab can disappear without saying goodbye, while a whiteboard still needs one ordered view of the document. The deciding constraint is trust. A client may draw a cursor, but it must not mint a channel token, widen its scope, or declare its own version current. A reconnect race can turn a harmless laptop sleep into a forked canvas. The fix is protocol work, not a longer timeout. Treat a channel as a lease with explicit states: requested, active, draining, and closed.
